adharabhuvi vedyarūpāyāṃ nipatanaṃ, tatra ayameva śūnyaprāṇabuddhidehābhidhānabhūmikāparigrahaḥ pūrvapūrvayogeneti īdṛśa eva kramaḥ | tathāhi vedyarūpe'pi nabhasi sarvāvakāśasahiṣṇutvaṃ vyāpakatvaṃ ceti na atyantamiva jaḍatā, tato vaibhavarahite vāyau spandaśaktimaye gaganāviyogini nīrūpe, tato rūpavati prakāśamaye tejasi, tataḥ prakāśaśūnye parapraveśakṣame ambhasi, tato'pi parapraveśāsahiṣṇāvatighane [ghane pārthive ga. |] sthūle pārthive atyantajaḍe pramātṛtābhimānaḥ krameṇa nikarṣadaśāmadhiśete | tatra kevalaśūnyasya ayogibhiravyavahāryatvāt lokāpekṣayā sparśamayasya prāṇasyaiva parigṛhītaśūnyānuvedhasya tejaḥsaṃbandhādhikyopanatacarācaradagdhṛtvasya prāthamyamucyate | tena saṃvidaḥ pariṇāmo hastina iva taṭe gāḍhena abhiniveśena anātmani vedyarūpe saṃkramaṇam | sa dehādyapekṣayā pūrvaṃ prāṇa ityucyate, antaḥkaraṇasya saṃkalpanābhimanananiścayanavṛttimayasya tattvam | yadanugrahādevaṃvidhavṛttilābhaḥ; tat cittattvaṃ, tasya vāyuḥ prāṇa āśrayatvamadhiṣṭheyatvaṃ gataḥ | tathābhūtena saṃvittattvādhiṣṭhitena prāṇena buddhirūpapuryaṣṭakasāhityabhājā yato'dhiṣṭhitaṃ śarīraṃ, tataścetanocitasvātantryayogo'sya; natu sākṣātsaṃvedanena adhiṣṭhitaṃ, tat | tathā ca uktaṃ prakāśarūpo bhagavān prāṇādhiṣṭhāna ucyate | prāṇa eva khago dharmo haṃsaśceti trivāhanaḥ || iti | ata eva śarīraṃ yadavāpnoti yaccāpyutkrāmatīśvaraḥ | gṛhītvaitāni saṃyāti vāyurgandhānivāśayāt | (15|8) iti bhagavatā [bhagavadgītāsu ga. |] gītāsu saṃvidrūpasya īśvarasya prāṇapuryaṣṭakādhiṣṭhānadvāreṇa (page 301) dehādhiṣṭhānatvamuktam, spandaśāstre'pi guruṇā yataḥ karaṇavargo'yaṃ vimūḍho'mūḍhavatsvayam | sahāntareṇa cakreṇa pravṛttisthitisaṃhṛtīḥ || labhate............................................................. **The Lord descends through the states, and deals with the world** The consciousness does not remain aloof. It descends, step by step, into the forms of the world — and this descent is the story of the bound knower. Abhinavagupta traces it through the states. The consciousness, entering the known-form, takes up the void, the breath, the intellect, the body, in order. Even space, the most permissive of forms, is not wholly inert; the wind, with its power of movement, less so; the light, with its form and brilliance, still less; the water, which receives what enters it; and finally the coarse, dense earth, the most inert of all. And with each descent, the self-conceit sinks further — as the elephant sinks into the mud-bank — until the consciousness comes to identify itself with the coarse body. For the world, the first of these is the breath (prāṇa): the touch-form, the moving, that takes up the void-following and, with the fire-connection, presides over the rest. The consciousness-tattva is what presides over the prāṇa, which presides over the intellect, the puryaṣṭaka (the inner city), and the body. So the Lord, the consciousness-form, presides over the body *through* the prāṇa and the puryaṣṭaka — not directly, by a bare experience, but as the inner light that animates them. As the Gītā says, "whatever body the Lord attains, and whatever he departs, taking these, he goes, as the wind takes the fragrances from the flower-bed." The īśvara, the consciousness-form, goes from body to body through the prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka, as the wind carries the scents. And the Spandakārikā's "with the inner wheel" is this same prāṇa, by which the organ-group obtains its proceeding, standing, and withdrawal. And because the consciousness, through the prāṇa, presides over the states, the enjoyment continues even after the body's death. As in the dream — the state immersed in sleep, the delusion — the prāṇa-embraced puryaṣṭaka, being the same, passes on, and the enjoyment in the other world, by the presiding over another body, is not impossible. The yogins are seen, remaining in their own body and their own house, to be elsewhere — proving the consciousness's power to preside beyond the present body. This leads to the kārikās. The construction (vikalpa, kārikā 6) is the joining of the "this" from the prior appearance, by the impression — it rests in the different manifestations, and it is a construction. But the *continuity* (anusandhāna) — the self that runs through the body, mind, breath, through all the states, from life to life — is not a construction; it is the one consciousness, un-divided. And in the dealing (kārikā 7), the Lord, entering the body, manifests the inner object-mass without, by the will. The world we deal with is the Lord's own inner mass, manifested outward by his will, through the very states through which he descends. And this is the kṛtyapañcaka — the fivefold work. The Lord creates, causes to stand, withdraws, conceals, and graces — and all five are his dealing, his manifestation of the inner mass through the states. The consciousness that descends through the void, the breath, the intellect, and the body is the same Lord who creates and deals with the whole world. The bound knower's descent is the Lord's descent; the dealing is the Lord's dealing; and the fivefold work is the Lord's own manifestation, through the prāṇa and the puryaṣṭaka, of the inner world without. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
